questions.question: Explain the biological role of haemoglobin in blood. What is carboxy haemoglobin, and why is carbon monoxide poisoning fatal?
questions.solution:
**Haemoglobin** is the red iron-containing pigment of red blood corpuscles, with the formula $C_{2952}H_{4664}N_{812}O_{832}S_{8}Fe_4$. It is a conjugated protein in which each of the four $Fe^{2+}$ ions is held inside a porphyrin ring called **haem**, the combination being haemoglobin.

**Biological role.** It transports oxygen from the lungs to all the tissues of the body, and also carries some carbon dioxide back. Oxygen binds reversibly to $Fe^{2+}$:

$$\text{Hb} + 4\text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Hb(O}_2)_4$$

**Carboxy haemoglobin.** Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin to form a stable cherry-red compound:

$$\text{Hb} + 4\text{CO} \rightarrow \text{Hb(CO)}_4 \qquad (\text{carboxyhaemoglobin})$$

**Why it is fatal.** CO binds to the $Fe^{2+}$ of haemoglobin about **250 times more avidly** than oxygen does, and the complex formed is far more stable and is not readily dissociated. Even a small concentration of CO in air (about 0.1%) saturates the haemoglobin completely, so no oxygen can reach the tissues. This produces severe hypoxia of all the tissues and organs, leading to unconsciousness and death within a few minutes.
questions.knowledgeNote: Haemoglobin carries O₂ through Fe²⁺; CO binds about 250 times more strongly, forming carboxyhaemoglobin that cannot release oxygen.
